Case study 01
Collections 0 → 1 Android · Web B2B SaaS

Streamlining Loan Collections Process at Olyv

The existing collections process at Olyv was being run on Excel sheets. There was a lot of ambiguity around what steps were being followed to collect money back from the user. We decided to change that and make the process more streamlined, for better tracking and clear transparency. The Android app took me 3 weeks of design and research, and the product is currently live in specific regions.

My role
Solo. Research to handoff.
Timeline
3 weeks
Platform
Android APK · Web · iOS webview
Status
Live. Agents onboarding.
Highlights
Context

What was actually happening before this existed

When someone stops paying their loan EMIs, Olyv sends their details to regional third party collection companies to recover the loan amount. These agents are incentivised per visit, and on the total amount they collect from users each day.

The entire process was being run on Excel sheets, where there was no way for Olyv to verify that a visit actually happened. So we decided to build a product that would remove the ambiguity altogether.

Before

Agents filled in their Excel sheet at their own pace

No way to verify that a visit actually happened

Incentives were being paid out for fraudulent cases too

No single place or platform for Olyv to track metrics

After

Every visit is logged in a timely manner

Location access helps us ensure that a visit was actually made

Incentivisation is transparent and very streamlined

Data gets mapped daily to Olyv's internal dashboard for easier tracking

Research

Link between Olyv & user (loan borrower)

It was important for me to understand how collections actually worked. Hence, I sat down with PMs from the Collections team to understand the workflow, and here's what I found:

Olyv Lending Platform No transparency into progress
Agency manager & Supervisor Third party No clarity on how data & cases are split
Field agent Third party No proof the visit was made
User Loan borrower

For Phase 1, we decided to design only for agents, since they're the actual touchpoint with the user. The project had to be made scalable in such a way that the same can be replicated for supervisors and managers too, in the next phase.

Research

There was nothing to audit, so I talked to people

No existing product meant no screens to critique. I called agents, used FOS tools that already existed in the market, and spent a lot of time talking to the PMs and engineers who'd been working with these agencies for years.

Talked to agents

Called a few agents into our office to understand what their day actually looked like — how they used Excel, and how they planned their routes each day around the cases they were assigned.

Analysed competitors

Went through existing FOS apps to see how others in the industry were solving this. I didn't have direct access, so I studied the apps on agents' own phones and through YouTube videos.

Spoke to PMs and devs

Needed to understand what was feasible to build in a limited timeframe with limited resources. They also handled agents' day-to-day queries, so they knew the pain points.

Mapped the entire flow

Mapped a rough workflow for every level of access — manager, supervisor, and agent — to find the gaps that could be plugged.

What came up

Agents were used to existing industry apps

As third-party contractors, agents also collected for many other NBFCs. Not every company had its own platform, so they used common industry tools — meaning agents were already fluent in a range of existing apps. Our workflow couldn't stray too far from what they knew, without compromising on any requirement.

Agents visited areas with poor signal

This came up with almost everyone. Because of weak signal, agents often filled in data only after returning to the office — making it very hard to verify whether they'd actually visited the borrower or were faking it for incentives. In the existing data, ~40% of visits logged in Excel were faked to over-claim incentives.

Nobody trusted how incentives were calculated

Agents had no clarity on how, or how much, they'd be paid — per case or per collection. They wanted to see money credited to their account in real time. This ambiguity had to go.

Agents found it hard to reach Olyv

For every "User Found" and PTP (promise-to-pay) case, agents had to contact our collections team for loan-settlement offers, penalty waivers, or EMI discounts. It was slow — they'd wait 4+ minutes on an IVR before reaching an agent, all while standing next to the borrower they'd come to collect from.

Constraints

Things I had to work around

No user photos allowed

Compliance gave a hard no. They wanted to be certain agents couldn't use borrowers' personal details as leverage against people who owed large amounts. It would have helped with identification, but it simply wasn't an option.

No reliable signal or internet

Agents work where connectivity is unpredictable, and capturing data at the borrower's doorstep was crucial. I worked with the tech team on a way for the app to function offline and sync once signal returned.

Limited dev bandwidth

Stakeholders didn't want to pour time and effort into a tool for agents rather than revenue-generating consumers. So it had to be built without consuming much tech or dev bandwidth.

Location capture was a necessity

Cutting fraudulent entries meant shifting agent behaviour. We introduced location capture at the moment of the visit — an agent earned the incentive for a visit only if they shared location access while there.

Basic phone setup

Many agents carried two phones — a personal one and a basic device for field work. Every component had to be small and quick so the app stayed fast on those basic phones, even on weak networks.

Access for managers and supervisors

The design had to scale so managers and supervisors could be onboarded too, assigning cases to agents directly. The app was built from the ground up with that in mind.

Design decisions

The decisions I kept coming back to

With three weeks to ship, I had to be clear about what actually mattered. These three kept coming up.

The problem

How do we make sure the visit actually happened, and that the agent logged the correct outcome?

What I did

After thorough brainstorming with the tech team, we settled on two things: mandatory location sharing, and photo capture with pre-tagged geolocation.

How it helped

Agents can't enter false data just to claim an incentive. Location access confirmed the agent was actually within 200m of the user's address. Geo-tagging the photos helped in two ways: we had proof the agent really visited (the images will be parsed in V2), and a different agent visiting the same address later would know what the location looks like.

The problem

Settlement offers and discounts on penalties were common use cases, but how do I handle a partial payment from the user?

What I did

We defined the situations that could come up and landed on 7 cases for calls and 8 for field visits. For example, PHONE_PICKED for a call and RTP_USER_FOUND for a field visit.

How it helped

The partial-payment case, and every other case, was handled cleanly, so the agent didn't have to struggle with the app while logging a visit right at the user's doorstep.

The problem

Incentives for every case were dynamic, so we couldn't show a single static value across all cases to every agent.

What I did

Since every case carried a different level of priority, the incentives varied too. I surfaced the incentive for each case right on the landing page, so agents could decide which cases to prioritise.

How it helped

Incentives were higher for cases with larger pending recovery amounts, so the chances of recovering at least some amount went up, and the company benefited too.

Benchmarking

How others are doing it

We decided to analyse other apps in the market that were already being used by collection agencies, to get a fair idea of what features they offered, how they tracked agents, and what information they were showcasing to the agents.

Design

Field Visit Scenarios

During discussion with agents in the office, I was able to categorise all the scenarios that can occur during a visit into 8 tags. I decided to show these tags alongside every visit in the history, so an agent knows what happened if the same user was visited by someone else before.

PAID_ON_VISIT

The user cleared the overdue amount during the visit. The agent records how it was paid and the case closes.

ALREADY_PAID

The user had already settled the dues before the agent arrived, so there was nothing left to collect.

PTP_USER_FOUND

Promised to pay. The user was found and committed to paying within a set time, so a reminder is scheduled and the case stays open.

RTP_USER_FOUND

Refused to pay. The user was found but declined to clear the overdue amount.

NCB_USER_NOT_FOUND

The agent reached the location but couldn't find the user at all, with no sign they'd moved and no problem with the address.

UNF_ADDRESS_CORRECT

User not found. The address was correct, but the user wasn't there at the time of the visit.

NCB_USER_RELOCATED

The agent reached the location and confirmed the user had relocated to a different address.

NCB_ADDRESS_INCORRECT

The address on file turned out to be incorrect, so the user couldn't be located there.

Design

An app for the field, a dashboard for the desk

The Android app is what agents use when they're standing at someone's door. The web dashboard is for when they're back at a desk, or for the small number of agents on iPhones. Both do the same thing — I just had to design them for very different contexts.

Android app
In the field
Big tap targets — used while moving, sometimes one-handed
High contrast everywhere — readable in sunlight
Saves offline, uploads when signal comes back
Location captured automatically when a case is opened
Everything reachable from the bottom of the screen
No camera access
Web dashboard
At a desk, or iOS
Full case list with search and filtering
Same visit flow as the app — no separate version
Summary of visits, amounts, and estimated payout
Works in a mobile browser for iPhone users
Laid out so supervisor views can be added later without restructuring
Design

Reworking the agent's landing page

The case list is the first thing an agent opens every morning, and it shapes the whole day. My first iteration worked, but it treated every case the same and hid what agents reach for most. Four things changed that.

1

Cases split by their status

The first iteration had every status sitting in the same scroll, on one page. After several rounds of iteration and usability testing, it now has three tabs to toggle between: Assigned Cases, Cases in Progress, and Collected.

2

Primary actions on every card, upfront

Agents needed to call the user to check they were at the location before making a visit. So it made sense to surface these two CTAs, Call User and Visit Location, upfront for easier access.

3

Incentive for every case, upfront

The first iteration didn't have an incentive component at all. To improve transparency, we decided to show the incentive for every case upfront, so agents can choose which ones to visit first.

4

Easier sorting and filtering

This was a big piece of feedback from usability testing. Quite a few agents missed the filters on the first screen unless we asked them to look, so we made it far more prominent, which made their work easier.

The agent app, step by stepscroll to see all 6 steps
01

Sign in with phone & OTP

Agents sign in with their phone number and a one-time password. Only numbers already registered with Olyv can get in. There are no open sign-ups.

02

Land on the allocated case list

The homepage lists every case allocated to the agent, split across Assigned, In Progress, and Collected, with search up top.

03

Open a case and review the data

Opening a case shows the full picture: borrower details, loan amount and overdue, previous audits, and the payment offers available to help close it.

04

Choose the audit type

For each user the agent picks how they're recording the interaction: a call audit, or a field visit, which is the one that carries an incentive.

05

Share location for a field visit

Choosing a field visit asks for location access. The incentive only counts when the agent is actually near the borrower's registered address.

06

Log the visit details

Finally, the agent logs the outcome: PTP, the borrower's phone number, visit address, photos, and amount collected.

What's next

Built for agents now. Room for everyone else later.

Phase 1 focused on the agents, the touchpoint our loan borrowers interact with directly. Supervisors and managers come next, and eventually the tool opens up to other lenders too.

Phase 1

Agents

Solving the problems at the very touchpoint our loan borrowers interact with directly.

Live now
Phase 2

Supervisors & Managers

Improving the shortcomings from Phase 1 after feedback from agents, and implementing the system for supervisors and managers together, so they can share data directly on the app.

Up next
Phase 3

A standalone collections product

Releasing the tool as a separate product into the collections market, so other companies can use it as their own collections platform.

Roadmap
Outcome

Product is currently Live.

The product has been live for 2 weeks in certain regions of India. The metrics are being tracked successfully, and adoption among agents is slowly increasing as the product rolls out to more of them.

What's different now

Agents can't fake a visit anymore

Location sharing ensures such fraudulent issues don't arise anymore. We expect these cases to drop from 40% to a far lower number.

Complete transparency

We're able to see what data is being added to the platform in real time, and how agents are using the app. It can be made even better in Phase 2.

No confusion over incentivisation

Every visit shows its corresponding incentive, which brings complete clarity on how agents are paid. No confusion anymore.

Loan borrower's privacy is still ensured

Since the user's photograph is never shared with agents, there's no chance of it being misused to pressure someone during a collection.

Futurescope

What's next for the project?

01

Watch Clarity videos and track agent behaviour to improve the application further

We need to ensure the app is running as intended, since the company wants to offer this as a B2B SaaS product in the future. We'll implement Microsoft Clarity on the app to give us live data on how users explore it and move through the intended flows.

02

Scale this to 100% of third party agents

The app is to be released to all agents collecting due amounts from Olyv users. The rollout across all agencies will happen once the initial dataset verifies that the app and its flows work, and any necessary changes have been made.

03

Build for supervisors and managers

The product needs to be scaled so the app can roll out across the entire agency, with everything in Olyv's loan recovery process happening through this one app.

04

Offer it as an individual product to other companies

The end goal is to license it to other quick loan service companies or NBFCs, so they can use the app for their own loan recovery process too.
